extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of constitutional/political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the conditions, qualities, and cautions the author identifies as necessary for elective and cabinet government to function well (e.g., mutual trust, calm national mind, competent legislature, deferential culture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual local political trust (political credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best political credit is analogous to mercantile credit; we trust our countrymen without remembering that we trust them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust tends to be strong among immediate neighbours and weak toward remote regions: 'the immemorial boundary mark begins in feeling a strange world.' Effective cooperation (even on trivial matters) across distant regions is difficult where locality is a passion; indirect/latent electoral processes help mask and sustain the political trust necessary for representative government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm national mind (stability to bear revolutionary excitement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A calm national mind — a tone of mind sufficiently stable to bear the necessary excitement of conspicuous revolutions — is a rare condition for elective government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uneducated or barbarous masses cannot be told to 'go and choose your rulers' without risk of violent usurpation. August institutions (visible unchosen rulers) prevent collapse by channeling reverence; the separation between 'reigning' and 'governing' (e.g., a monarch as symbol) dampens destabilising excitement among poorer, less informed classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationality (capacity to form distant conceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole people electing its rulers must be able to form a distinct conception of distant objects — a quality the author calls 'rationality' (distinct from mere intelligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular deification of a king prevents the steady conception needed for electoral choice; only in a world with wider experience and colder thought does the plain rule of a palpably chosen ruler become possible. Rationality enables citizens to grasp and evaluate those who govern from afar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of a competent legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet government requires not only elective government's conditions but also 'the possibility likewise of a good legislature — a legislature competent to elect a sufficient administration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A competent legislature must exist (i.e., a continuous mechanism for enacting and repealing laws) and be willing and able to select and sustain an efficient executive; the rarity of continuous legislatures explains the relative rarity of true cabinet systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous (permanently acting) legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: A permanent, constantly acting mechanism for enacting and repealing laws is a necessary condition for cabinet government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early societies prized fixed law and would find a continuously active legislature anomalous; only in civilised communities, where legal adaptation is necessary, is continuous legislation feasible and supportive of cabinet government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness of legislature to elect and maintain an efficient executive
rubrics_metrics.description: A competent legislature must be willing to elect and willing to maintain an efficient administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence is not merely structural; a legislature must have the disposition and political habit of choosing and defending capable ministers. Without willingness, even formally competent institutions will fail to produce stable cabinets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient supply of substantial non-elective business
rubrics_metrics.description: To keep a legislature efficient it must have a sufficient supply of substantial business; lacking this, members will quarrel about trivialities and elective business, producing feeble administrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When great questions end and there are few laws to enact or repeal, parliament may waste itself on ministerial quarrels; a parliament with little business must be intrinsically much better in other respects to remain effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffused education and material comfort among the mass
rubrics_metrics.description: One path to a good legislature is a nation where the mass of people are intelligent and comfortable — education diffused, no 'honest poverty', and political intelligence common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conditions (exemplified in some North American states) make it easier for the populace to elect a fair legislature; dispersed populations can impede discussion, but overall diffused comfort and education produce political capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferential national character
rubrics_metrics.description: A cabinet government can also arise in deferential nations where the numerous unwiser part wishes to be ruled by a less numerous wiser part — the masses voluntarily delegate choice to an educated minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference enables selection of a competent legislature even where the mass is not well-educated. England is held up as the archetype, where mass deference is sustained by social spectacle, visibility of elites, and traditional respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility/theatrical spectacle of elites and monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'theatrical show of society' — pomp, spectacle, visible courts and aristocracy culminating in a monarch — generates imaginative deference among the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visibility (not necessarily intellectual merit) constrains and guides popular imagination, making people accept the authority of nominal electors and obscure real rulers operating behind the spectacle; it is an important mechanism by which deference is produced and maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability risk of ignorant but deferential masses
rubrics_metrics.description: A deferential community whose bulk are ignorant is in 'unstable equilibrium': if the equilibrium is once disturbed and the ignorant begin to rule, deference may be lost forever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once deference is challenged and popular organs take control, a people rarely accepts being ruled again by the formerly respected minority; demagogues and sympathetic popular press prevent recognition that the dethroned elite governed better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural-historical prerequisites (tradition and custom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical conditions — tradition, transmitted reverence, and the social habit of respecting established classes — are prerequisites for sustaining deference and certain constitutional forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect is often traditional rather than merit-based; in new colonies lacking such traditions, deference must be proven by the elite and is hard to establish. Early societies often valued fixed law over good law, impeding continuous legislative development.
